name: Fitbone nail

card.summary: A fully implantable, motorised lengthening rod placed inside the thigh or shin bone that gradually lengthens the bone, used to add leg length and, in cosmetic cases, height.
card.note: Major orthopaedic surgery with a reported complication rate of roughly a third of lengthened segments in one systematic review.

quick.overview:
The Fitbone is a motorised intramedullary nail made by the German company Wittenstein. It is implanted inside the marrow canal of the femur or tibia, the bone is cut, and the nail is then lengthened in small daily steps so new bone forms in the gap. Surgeons use it mainly for leg-length differences and deformity, and it is also used in cosmetic height-increase lengthening.

Because the device sits entirely inside the bone and is driven through the skin by a radio-frequency transmitter, it avoids the external frames and pins of older methods. Published case series and reviews describe lengthening of several centimetres per segment, with complication and mechanism-failure rates reported in the literature.
quick.how: The procedure is performed by orthopaedic limb-reconstruction surgeons under general anaesthesia. After the bone is cut and the nail is placed, a short waiting period is followed by a distraction phase in which a patient-operated external transmitter triggers the motor, typically around a millimetre a day. A longer consolidation period follows while the new bone hardens, with physiotherapy throughout, and the nail is later removed in a second operation.
quick.risks: A 2021 systematic review of 983 lengthened segments (FITBONE and PRECICE nails) reported complications in 34% of segments, mostly minor to moderate, with permanent problems in about 3%. Reported risks include delayed or poor bone healing, joint stiffness, nerve or vascular injury, infection, and device failure. It is a major surgery with a long recovery, and cosmetic lengthening is regulated differently in different countries.

lead: The Fitbone nail is a fully implantable, motorised intramedullary lengthening device developed and sold by Wittenstein. It is inserted into the medullary canal of the femur or tibia, and after the bone is surgically divided it can be extended in controlled increments from outside the body, so that the bone gradually grows longer through distraction osteogenesis [1][2]. For people seeking more height, it offers a way to add leg length without an external fixator frame.

Clinically the nail is used for limb-length discrepancy, congenital shortening, deformity correction and short stature, and also for bone transport in defects [3][4]. In height-focused communities it is discussed as one of the internal-nail options for cosmetic lengthening alongside the magnetically driven PRECICE nail, valued because there are no pins through the skin and, in published series, patients describe it as more comfortable than older systems [5].

Research consists largely of case series, retrospective cohort comparisons and systematic reviews rather than randomised trials. A 2021 systematic review pooled 214 Fitbone segments with PRECICE segments, and a 2026 review of 2,495 nails analysed mechanism failures [6][7].

chain: Bone in the thigh or shin is divided and the nail inserted
Motor lengthens the nail in small daily steps
New bone forms in the gap
Longer femur or tibia adds standing height
angle.text: The nail lengthens the leg bone itself, so the added length is permanent once the bone has healed. People use it for cosmetic height gain or to even out leg lengths, with the amount of lengthening planned by the surgeon for each bone.

paras: The Fitbone is described as a fully implantable, motorised lengthening and correction nail. It combines an intramedullary rod with a telescoping mechanism, and power and control signals are transmitted through the skin so no part of the device crosses the skin [8]. Reported advantages of internal nails over external frames include avoiding pin-site infection, less scarring and less muscle and joint tethering [5].

Unlike purely mechanical ratchet nails that required the patient to rotate the limb to advance the mechanism, motor-driven nails are lengthened at a controlled rate, which reviews link to less pain during lengthening and better control over the rate [5].

Limb lengthening by distraction was proposed in the 19th century, attempted clinically in 1905 by Alessandro Codivilla, and became widespread after Gavriil Ilizarov developed his external fixation system from the 1950s [8]. Intramedullary solutions were explored from the 1970s onward, and motorised implantable nails such as the Fitbone emerged in the 2000s [9][10].

Early series reported use in non-traumatic disorders, including short stature and Ollier's disease, in adults and adolescents [10][11]. Reports from centres in several countries, including a first French experience and adolescent femoral series, followed [12][13]. Review authors describe the shift to intramedullary lengthening nails as one of the largest changes in managing limb-length discrepancy since distraction osteogenesis was adopted in the West [14].

Lengthening proceeds in phases: surgery to cut the bone and insert the nail, a latency period of about a week, a distraction phase at roughly one millimetre per day, a consolidation phase while the bone hardens, and a later operation to remove the implant [8]. Surgeons also use planning methods to correct angular deformity at the same time as lengthening [15].

Cosmetic limb lengthening has been reported in several countries. Wikipedia notes demand in India, where the industry is described as unregulated, and that China's health ministry banned the procedure in 2006 after serious complications. Patients interviewed in news coverage have described infections, further surgery and less height gained than expected [8].

Published nail series include patients operated for short stature, with one early series of ten patients including six with short stature [11]. In height communities, the Fitbone is often compared with PRECICE; a retrospective comparison of 41 patients with the two nails examined clinical, radiological and functional results [16].

A systematic review of 983 segments lengthened with FITBONE or PRECICE found complications in 34% of segments: 11% minimal-intervention, 15% requiring a substantial change in treatment, 5% failure to reach the goal and 3% new pathology or permanent sequelae [6].

A 2026 review of 29 studies covering 2,495 nails reported an overall mechanism-related failure rate of 4.3%, with different failure patterns by implant material [7]. A study of 128 Fitbone nails reported no osteolysis at the telescopic junction [17]. Compared with external frames, a paediatric comparison in congenital femoral deficiency examined complications of the Fitbone against circular fixation [18].

Most evidence is observational. A series of 32 consecutive patients (median age 17) lengthened with the Fitbone reported successful lengthening in 30 of 32 cases [19]. A series of ten adolescents examined lower-limb lengthening and deformity correction with the nail [20]. A 2020 meta-analysis of motorised internal lengthening versus other techniques examined union time and length achieved [21].
A registered post-market study of patient pain, satisfaction and quality of life with the Fitbone began recruiting in 2024 [22].
